# evoq {#sec-evoq}

The framework on top of reckon-db. Aggregates, projections, subscriptions, snapshots — the artefacts that make a Division a Division.

## What this chapter will cover

### The 21 behaviours

evoq is a collection of Erlang behaviours, each of which formalises one role in a Division. The chapter walks the load-bearing ones.

| Behaviour | Role |
|---|---|
| `evoq_aggregate` | The Dossier's command-handling brain |
| `evoq_decision` | The Decision pattern (Chapter 5) |
| `evoq_projection` | A read-model materialiser |
| `evoq_event_handler` | A consumer of events with retry / DLQ |
| `evoq_process_manager` | A saga-style coordinator |
| `evoq_adapter` | The event-store backend (`reckon_evoq` plugs reckon-db in) |
| `evoq_subscription_adapter` | The subscription backend |
| `evoq_snapshot_adapter` | The snapshot backend |
| `evoq_checkpoint_store` | Where projection checkpoints live |

Plus twelve more for less-frequently-extended roles (upcasters, middleware, idempotency stores, dead-letter handlers, etc.).

### Why behaviours

- They are the *contract*, not the *implementation*. The Codex names what each role does; the behaviour is the Erlang artefact that captures the contract.
- Substituting one implementation for another (different backend, different retry strategy) is a one-line dependency change.
- Compile-time enforcement of callback shape catches a class of integration bugs early.

### The aggregate lifecycle

Initialised → loaded from history → command received → validated → events appended → idle → passivated → re-loaded. Configurable TTL. Memory-pressure-aware passivation.

### The projection contract

Subscribes via the subscription adapter. Receives events in order. Updates a read model. Persists checkpoints so it can resume after a restart. Idempotent against redelivery.

### The Decision runtime

`evoq_decision_runtime:dispatch/3` runs the read-decide-write loop with bounded retry and exponential backoff. Cross-reference Chapter 5.
